contributions.headingText: The fibrolamellar variant of hepatocellular carcinoma (FLHCC) is a primary malignancy of the liver composed of epithelial cells showing hepatocellular differentiation with characteristic morphological features and recurrent genomic abnormalities typically involving the PRKACA gene.
2C12.02 & XH9Q35 Hepatocellular carcinoma of liver & Hepatocellular carcinoma, fibrolamellar
FLHCC can occur in any portion of the liver but is most common in the left lobe {6248194}, and it has a propensity to involve the hilum.

Patients present with an abdominal mass or hepatomegaly, and/or with otherwise nonspecific symptoms including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, malaise, and weight loss {17452818}. Less common are mass effects due to the tumour, including biliary or vena caval obstruction. Rarely, FLHCC may occur with gynaecomastia, recurrent deep vein thrombosis, Budd–Chiari syndrome, non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis, fulminant liver failure, or encephalopathy {1337896; 2841641; 20010160}. Other uncommon clinical features include increased serum neurotensin or increased serum transcobalamin 1 (TCN1, also called haptocorrin) {28110996}.

Patients with FLHCC typically do not have underlying liver disease, and almost all cases (95%) arise in non-cirrhotic livers. No elevation in serum AFP is seen. Lymphatic spread is common, as are peritoneal spread and lymphovascular invasion {11012437; 16475212; 9328308; 10025374; 7717223}. Ovarian metastasis has been reported {22296446}.

Imaging

On CT, FLHCC is usually a large, heterogeneous, well-defined mass that is predominantly hypoattenuating on unenhanced images {10551212; 2997835}. Calcification is seen in 50% of cases {10551212; 2997835}. Although a central stellate scar is seen in two thirds of FLHCCs {10551212; 11997564}, it is not pathognomonic. On MRI, FLHCC is usually hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images {10551212}. The central scar is typically hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images, a feature that can help distinguish FLHCC from focal nodular hyperplasia (in which the scar is predominantly T2-hyperintense) {24555590}. With gadolinium contrast, FLHCC shows arterial hyperenhancement and early venous washout {24555590; 32102105}.

FLHCC accounts for 15–25% of paediatric hepatocellular carcinomas (HCCs) and is exclusive to children aged > 5 years {24439603}. Children with FLHCC are older than those with HCC (88% vs 29% aged > 12 years, respectively), and unlike in HCC there is no male predominance {23683550}.

Activation of PKA (a tetramer composed of two regulatory and two catalytic subunits) via the increased activity of PRKACA appears to be a central mechanism in FLHCC tumorigenesis. In nearly all sporadic cases, this activation occurs through a DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion, which results from a 400 kb deletion of chromosome 19 {24578576}. The fusion transcript leads to increased PKA Cα subunit expression and PKA activity. Studies in mice have shown that the fusion transcript is sufficient to induce hepatic tumours that are morphologically similar to FLHCC {28923495}.

The DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion is present in the vast majority of cases of FLHCC, but rare cases have been reported that lack the fusion and instead demonstrate mutations in PRKAR1A. The majority of these cases occur in patients with Carney complex, 60–70% of whom have a germline mutation in PRKAR1A {29222914}. PRKAR1A is the regulatory subunit of PKA {24578576}, the loss of which results in a gain of PRKACA function {11115848}.

Although cytogenetic changes have been reported in FLHCC, no recurrent structural abnormalities other than the deletion in chromosome 19 have been identified {25605237}. FLHCC lacks the common gene alterations seen in conventional HCC, including in TP53 and CTNNB1.

Most tumours are solitary and large (range: 90–140 mm) at the time of resection {9328308}. Tumours consist of well-circumscribed, multinodular, yellow to tan to green masses that may range from soft to firm to hard in consistency. Cut sections reveal a central scar in approximately 70% of cases {10551212}. Gross vascular invasion may be seen (25% of cases) {9328308}. The background liver is non-cirrhotic.

FLHCC consists of large polygonal cells with vesicular nuclear chromatin, prominent single nucleoli, and abundant granular and eosinophilic cytoplasm due to abundant mitochondria {6284337}, lysosomes {6284337}, and/or endosomal cytoplasmic accumulations {21113139}. Binucleated and multinucleated tumour cells can be seen. The tumour cells are arranged in trabeculae, cords, and nests in a dense fibrous stroma classically arranged in parallel lamellae.

Other classic (but nonspecific) features of FLHCC include pale eosinophilic cytoplasmic bodies, thought to be composed at least partly of fibrinogen, and hyaline bodies, which may be seen in approximately 50% of cases.

Other features include calcifications, bile production, and pseudoglandular structures with mucin production, as well as solid and peliotic patterns.

Immunohistochemically, tumour cells express markers of hepatocellular differentiation, including HepPar-1 and arginase-1 (ARG1); albumin mRNA can be detected by in situ hybridization. FLHCC may show a canalicular staining pattern for polyclonal CEA. Glypican-3 (GPC3) positivity is also reported (in 17–64% of cases) {20444731; 18536657; 20495535}. AFP is usually negative. Characteristically, almost all cases (85–90%) of FLHCC demonstrate strong diffuse expression of CK7 and CD68 due to abundant lysosomes {28862261; 21113139}; these findings are also seen in conventional HCC (CK7 in 20–30% of cases {20444731; 20495535}; CD68 in 10–25% {21113139}). The expression of CK7 and CD68 may be patchy, and rare cases may be negative. FLHCC also stains for α1-antitrypsin and copper. It shows strong expression of AGR2 {18973922}. Rarely, expression of neuroendocrine markers is seen {1848288}. Other markers that may be positive in FLHCC but are not in routine diagnostic use include EpCAM, CD56 (NCAM), CD113, and CD44 {20495535}; liver fatty acid–binding protein expression may be absent {27015136}.

FLHCC is characterized by aggregates of loosely cohesive polygonal cells with large nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant oncocytic granular cytoplasm, which may contain pale bodies and hyaline bodies. Characteristic lamellar fibrosis may be seen within tumour fragments. A background of proliferating capillaries may be present {1698598; 11933273; 10450103; 2996274}.

The DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion can be detected by RT-PCR, or by FISH {25698061; 28862261}, which has a sensitivity of 97% and specificity of 100% for FLHCC in the context of a primary liver neoplasm {28862261}. The fusion is not specific to FLHCC and has been reported in pancreatobiliary malignancies {31676785}.

In the rare cases with mutations in PRKAR1A rather than the DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion, loss of PRKAR1A expression can be confirmed by immunohistochemistry {29222914}.

Essential: large polygonal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and macronucleoli; dense fibrosis; CK7 expression.

Desirable: demonstration of DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion.

The current staging system is the eighth-edition American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) or Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) system [[Amin MB, Edge S, Greene F, et al., editors. AJCC cancer staging manual. 8th ed. New York (NY): Springer; 2017.]]. However, studies have shown limitations in the predictive value of this system in FLHCC {27456016; 16475212; 24051705}. Other proposed staging systems include the pretreatment extent of disease (PRETEXT) system currently in use for hepatoblastoma {29427028}, including in the ongoing Paediatric Hepatic International Tumour Trial (PHITT).

In early studies of FLHCC, some showed that the survival of patients with FLHCC was better than that of patients with other HCC {6248194; 10025374; 6311397; 2981486}, whereas others did not {12673731; 23683550}. Subsequent larger case series and meta-analyses have shown that overall survival is similar between patients with FLHCC and those with conventional HCC {24799971; 27456016}. Likewise, studies of FLHCC in children have shown no differences in outcomes between FLHCC and other HCCs {12673731; 23683550}, with a reported 5-year event-free survival rate of 30% in US trials {12673731} and 3-year event-free and overall survival rates of 22% and 42%, respectively, in the SIOPEL studies {23683550}; cases in younger patients (aged < 12 years) and with no multifocality show a trend towards better outcomes {22981432}.

Cases of FLHCC with increased mitochondrial DNA levels {20228784} and those with a greater number of chromosomal imbalances {18997738} show aggressive behaviour.

Lymph node metastasis in FLHCC is common and does not affect prognosis {16475212; 27456016}. Adverse prognostic features include vascular invasion, multifocality, and incomplete surgical resectability, including resectability of regional lymph node metastases {24051705}. In children, FLHCC, like conventional HCC, has shown a poor response to chemotherapy, and the prognosis is determined by surgical resectability {12673731; 23683550}.
